newsitem.title: USA: Floods ease in parts of Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Floods ease in parts of Midwest.

text.p: An ice jam that had backed up the swollen Rock River broke on Wednesday and officials said floodwaters that had imprisoned two small Illinois towns were beginning to retreat.
But heavy rain was falling again, raising renewed fears of flooding in the central part of Illinois and farther down the Mississippi Valley watershed.
The Whiteside County Sheriff's Office said floodwaters were receding at the hamlets of Erie and Hillsdale, about 130 miles (210 km) west of Chicago.

"We will have some roads opened up later in the day," an emergency coordinator at the office said. Most of Hillsdale was evacuated but some Erie residents remained even as the town of 1,500 was surrounded by water from ice jams and broken levees.
The flooding was caused by a combination of a four-inch (10 cm) rainfall last week running off frozen ground that prevented absorption.
The Illinois River also overflowed its banks in many areas, including Peoria where bank-side homes north of the city were submerged.

Flood watches were issued from Texas north across Arkansas and Missouri into Illinois on Wednesday. As much as two inches (five cm) of rain was forecast across parts of the region, raising the threat of additional flooding.

"We do have another rain storm moving in and it looks like it's taking aim right at the Illinois River," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. The heaviest rainfall will be between Peoria and Springfield."

Burgio said "almost all of the rain that falls goes into the rivers. In the summertime a good portion of it is either absorbed into the soils and used by the vegetation or evaporated because of the hotter temperatures."
Mid-range forecasts suggested storms would cross Illinois about every third day, said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster with Weather Express Inc.
He said another rainstorm was possible on Saturday, dropping as much as two inches (5 cm).
"Temperatures are going to be mild enough with these systems that where there is snow, it's going to be melting," Gesser added. "It's (flooding) going to be worse before it gets better."
Heavy snow warnings were issued on Wednesday to the north of the rain belt.
